answer_text:
This is a great and insightful question! You've identified what seems like a mathematical impossibility, but in reality, several demographic, social, and biological factors combine to make polygyny (one man, multiple wives — the most common form of polygamy) function even with a roughly equal sex ratio at birth. Here's a detailed breakdown:

---

## 🔢 1. The Birth Ratio Isn't the Marriage Ratio

In human reproduction, slightly more male than female babies are born (approximately 105 boys to 100 girls). However, as boys are more likely to die of natural causes as infants and from violence before they marry and reproduce, at any given marriageable age, there will be approximately 50% males and 50% females. So the ratio evens out — but doesn't automatically create a surplus of women. That surplus comes from other factors:

---

## 👴👩 2. Men Marry Much Younger Women (Age Gap Effect)

This is the **single most important mechanism**. Polygynous marriage systems are maintained by a large gap between the ages at marriage of men and women, and the rapid remarriage of divorced and widowed women.

Here's why this creates an effective surplus of women: if older men are drawing from a pool of younger women, they are competing across **different age cohorts**. Polygynous marriage increases competition for wives, as married men remain on the marriage market. This increased competition drives down the age of first marriage for females and increases the spousal age gap. The reduced supply of unmarried women, who are absorbed into polygynous marriages, causes men of all ages to pursue younger and younger women.

Intrasexual competition for females increases as fewer females remain on the marriage market (with males having more than one wife each), therefore the competitive advantage values younger females due to their higher reproductive value. As the competition for younger women becomes more common, the age of females' first marriage lowers as older men seek younger and younger females.

In growing populations, this means there are always *more* young women entering marriageable age than older men from the same birth year — effectively creating an available pool.

---

## 📈 3. Population Growth Creates a Structural Surplus of Women

Real demography is not so simple. Women typically live longer than men, men frequently marry younger women, and populations in many parts of the world are growing, ensuring younger spouses are available for older cohorts. These factors, which are characteristic of many contemporary African nations, tilt the marriage market toward a surplus of women. Under many realistic conditions, a sizable proportion of men can have multiple wives without leaving their peers out in the cold.

Because younger age cohorts are larger in a growing population, there are always *more* young people than old people. When older men marry younger women, they are tapping into a numerically larger cohort — meaning there are genuinely more available young women than there are older men seeking them.

---

## 💀 4. Men Die Earlier, Creating a Literal Surplus of Older Women

Where mortality rates of men consistently exceed those of women, polygyny can be seen as a resolution to the "deficit" of males and the "surplus" of females.

Men die younger on average due to higher rates of violence, occupational hazards, and war. This means that over a lifetime, women outnumber men — especially in older age groups. Polygyny can be seen as a social structure that accommodates this imbalance.

---

## 💍 5. Widows and Divorcées Rapidly Remarry

Because it is possible, and often expected, for divorcees and widows to find new husbands in polygynous societies, women spend most of their fertile years in a marital union. This recycling of women back into the marriage pool effectively increases the number of women available for (re)marriage at any given time, boosting the functional supply without changing the biological sex ratio.

---

## 📊 6. Counterintuitively, Polygyny Doesn't Always Leave Men Unmarried

A landmark 2025 study published in PNAS confirmed this counterintuitive finding: in a wide range of demographic circumstances, polygyny can be practiced without any men in the population being locked out of marriage. The sustainable level of polygyny is generally higher when women live longer than men, since there will be more prospective brides than grooms.

In fact, in nearly half of the countries examined, higher rates of polygyny were associated with *fewer*, not more, unmarried men. Only a handful of countries showed the expected positive relationship, and even then inconsistently over time.

---

## ⚠️ 7. But It Does Create Real Problems

It's important to acknowledge that this system is not without serious consequences. So long as men may take more than one wife, and women may not do the same, and so long as the male-to-female sex ratio at the age of puberty is not much less than unity — a condition that is satisfied everywhere — then polygamy creates a chronic scarcity of marriageable females.

A suite of social conventions — such as age gaps at marriage, bride price, sequestration, and discrimination and violence against women — are overrepresented in polygamous societies as compared to monogamous societies. This dichotomy can be explained on the grounds that polygamy produces a chronic scarcity of marriageable females.

---

## Summary Table

| Factor | How it creates a functional surplus of women |
|---|---|
| **Age gap at marriage** | Older men draw from larger, younger female cohorts |
| **Population growth** | Younger cohorts are bigger, more women available |
| **Male higher mortality** | Fewer men survive to old age; more women remain |
| **Widow/divorcée remarriage** | Women re-enter the marriage pool quickly |
| **Cross-cohort competition** | Men marry across age groups, not just their own |

In short, the roughly 1:1 birth ratio is **not** the same as the marriage-market ratio. Demographic realities — especially age gaps, male mortality, and population growth — reshape the effective availability of women in ways that make polygyny mathematically sustainable, even if it comes with significant social costs.
